Neurology · published research

Olfactory dysfunction

In one 81-person post-COVID trial, the infrared PBM group improved UPSIT scores more than control at three months. Small traumatic and post-COVID studies also report changes, but they do not establish a general effect across causes of smell loss.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In one 81-person post-COVID trial, the infrared PBM group improved UPSIT scores more than control at three months. Small traumatic and post-COVID studies also report changes, but they do not establish a general effect across causes of smell loss.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact olfactory-dysfunction category contains two titles: one controlled human study of traumatic smell loss and one mouse study. A narrow adjacent-category mapping adds four post-COVID human publications, one systematic review and one related mouse study, for eight unique titles. The mapped human reports include one randomized trial, two other controlled or comparative studies, one case report and one case series. The review summarizes these records rather than adding a patient cohort.

Human and clinical evidence

Oliveira et al. randomized 81 people with persistent post-COVID smell loss to control, red light or infrared light. At three months, the infrared group improved its UPSIT smell-identification score by 4.6 points more than controls; the study also reported higher response rates in that arm (Oliveira et al. 2025). All groups also received corticosteroid treatment and olfactory training, and the trial was single-blinded, so the effect is an adjunctive result rather than a test of PBM alone. A 24-person study of traumatic olfactory loss reported changes in brain connectivity after laser treatment (Hosseini et al. 2023). A small post-COVID comparison and case reports describe smell or taste changes but are uncontrolled or combine outcomes (Panhoca et al. 2023 Soares et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

Two mouse publications study impaired olfaction after olfactory-bulb photothrombosis or ischemic stroke. The stroke paper reports earlier recovery on an olfactory task despite persistent infarction at follow-up (Shalaby et al. 2025). These models support biological questions but do not reproduce post-viral or traumatic human smell loss.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo olfactory-dysfunction study was identified in the mapped set.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The post-COVID randomized trial used intranasal red and infrared laser exposure twice weekly for five weeks, alongside olfactory training and corticosteroids. The traumatic study used red light around 660 nm, and the case series used intranasal PBM with different protocols. These routes and causes differ, and the study does not establish whether red and infrared light have the same effect.

Interpretation

The best direct evidence supports a short-term smell-test improvement from adjunctive infrared PBM in one post-COVID trial. It does not establish benefit for traumatic anosmia, other causes or persistence beyond the measured follow-up. Cause-specific studies and replication are needed to define how broadly the result applies.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow to moderate for three-month smell-test improvement with adjunctive intranasal infrared PBM after COVID-19, based on one randomized trial. Very low for traumatic smell loss, other causes or lasting benefit.
Publications and records8 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The strongest result is one 81-person randomized trial in post-COVID olfactory dysfunction, but it was single-blinded and all groups also received corticosteroid treatment and olfactory training. Other human reports are small or uncontrolled, and smell loss after trauma is a different condition. Independent trials should separate causes and follow smell function longer.
